visuals.title: The further down, the higher the return demanded
visuals.note: Illustrative. Senior lenders are paid first and hold security, so they accept the lowest rate.

visuals.at: Second trap. Losses aren't shared out evenly
visuals.title: Who gets what: losses hit the bottom first
visuals.note: Sofia's answer, everyone losing a sixth, would share the loss evenly. Claims are paid in order of priority instead.

visuals.at: So the sponsor fills the gap with layers below
visuals.title: The order of payment

items.label: Revolving facility and senior secured loans
items.detail: Paid first, secured on the assets, cheapest; usually floating rate

items.label: Second lien loans
items.detail: Secured, but behind the senior lenders

items.label: High-yield bonds
items.detail: Usually unsecured and fixed rate, with incurrence covenants

items.label: Mezzanine and PIK notes
items.detail: Interest often added to the debt rather than paid in cash

items.label: Equity
items.detail: Paid last, so it wants the highest return

visuals.note: The other ratio is leverage, debt ÷ EBITDA: 6x for Harbour, 4x of it senior.

visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Harbour has £400m of senior loans and £200m of bonds, and the business is worth £500m. How much do the bondholders get?
questions.explain: Losses are taken from the bottom up: the senior lenders get their £400m first, leaving £100m, or 50p in the pound, for the bonds. Sharing the loss evenly gives Sofia's £167m.
questions.explain_at: The bonds are owed two hundred and get the one hundred that's left

questions.q: Why do senior loans pay a lower rate than high-yield bonds?

options.text: They're paid first and secured on the assets
They're bigger, so they get a better rate
They pay a floating rate, so lenders accept less
Banks lend more cheaply than bond investors

questions.explain: Senior lenders take the least risk: they're first in line and hold security, so they accept the lowest return. Size has nothing to do with it.
questions.explain_at: Senior lenders are paid first and hold security

questions.q: Harbour issues £100m of PIK notes at 12% and pays no cash interest for five years. Roughly how much does it owe at the end?

options.text: £100m, as no cash interest is paid

questions.explain: The interest is added to the debt and compounds: 100 × 1.12⁵ ≈ 176. £160m is simple interest; £100m treats PIK as free money.
questions.explain_at: One hundred at twelve percent becomes one hundred and twelve

questions.q: GE Vernova says it's paying 13x EBITDA for Trench; the Börsen-Zeitung says 21x. Why the gap?

options.text: One is in dollars, the other in euros
They use EBITDA from different years

questions.explain: 13x is on expected 2028 EBITDA, which hasn't been earned yet; on this year's expected EBITDA the same price is about 19.5x. Same price, a different denominator.

questions.q: GE Vernova funds about half the price of Trench with debt. Why isn't that a leveraged buyout?

options.text: It is one: half the price is borrowed
The debt sits with GE Vernova, not Trench
Half is too little debt to count as leverage
Trench was already owned by a fund

questions.explain: The borrowing is GE Vernova's, backed by a far bigger group's earnings and kept below 1x EBITDA. An LBO loads the debt onto the target alone.
questions.explain_at: The debt sits with G-E Vernova, a far bigger company
